Monday, 8 January, nine o’clock. Radu and Chloé are starting their internship at Atelier Rhône. On the door, a new plaque: "Atelier Rhône — N. Fabre & I. Moreau-Popescu". Nathalie explains the rules to them.
Welcome, both of you. Right, a few rules. First, the hours: you have to be here at nine. Not ten past nine.
Understood. And in the evening, until what time do we have to stay?
You’re supposed to leave at six. But before a competition deadline, we sometimes have to stay later. I’ll let you know.
And for lunch? Are we allowed to eat here?
In the kitchen, yes. But it is strictly forbidden to eat in front of the computers. Last time, an intern spilled a coffee on a model. Three weeks of work.
(turns pale) No coffee near the models. Noted.
Each of you will have a tutor. Chloé will work with me. You, Radu, will work with Ioana.
With my sister? But… you said it was better if we didn’t work together.
I’ve changed my mind. The La Duchère project is hers to run, and it’s your drawing. It’s essential that you work together. But here, she isn’t your sister. She’s your tutor.
Do I have to call her "Madame"?
(laughs) You don’t have to go that far. But you have to accept her criticism without arguing. She’s demanding.
I know. She was already correcting my maths homework when I was eight.
Perfect, you’re used to it. One last thing: you have to hand in your first sketches on Friday. Claire Vasseur is coming to see them next Monday.
Welcome to the world of work, Radu. Here’s your badge. Don’t lose it: without it you can’t even get into the toilets.
supposed ("être censé" = to be supposed to)
right ("avoir le droit de" = to be allowed to)
was ("il valait mieux" = it was better)
haven’t ("tu n’as pas à" = you don’t have to)
habit ("avoir l’habitude" = to be used to)
"Eel foh": the final t is silent. In fast speech: "faut que…" = "foh-kuh".
"Sahn-say": nasal "ahn". Don’t confuse it with "sensé" (sensible), which sounds the same!
"Badzh": an English word, pronounced almost as in English.
"Il faut" is impersonal (it doesn’t change: there is no "je faut"). With the INFINITIVE it expresses a general obligation; with QUE + SUBJUNCTIVE, an obligation for a particular person:
Il faut que vous soyez à l’heure.
Il faut que tu acceptes ses critiques.

The typical Romanian mistake: "Je faut partir" (a calque of "trebuie"). "Falloir" only has the impersonal third person: il faut, il fallait, il faudra, il faudrait. The personal version: "je dois partir".
2. Devoir, être obligé de, avoir à
Vous devez rendre vos esquisses vendredi.
Tu n’as pas à aller jusque-là.
"Devoir" in the conditional (je devrais) is advice or a moral obligation: "Tu devrais appeler ta mère." = You should call your mother.
"Être censé + infinitive" means what SHOULD happen in principle (according to the rule or the plan), but doesn’t always happen. English says "to be supposed to":
You’re supposed to leave at six.
The train was supposed to arrive at noon.
I’m not supposed to know that.
4. Necessity and advice: il vaut mieux, il est nécessaire
All these impersonal expressions have the same structure: + DE + infinitive (general) or + QUE + subjunctive (for someone):
Il vaut mieux que tu demandes avant.
Il est indispensable que vous travailliez ensemble.
Il est important que tout le monde soit là.
Careful: "il vaut mieux" is followed directly by the infinitive, without "de": "Il vaut mieux partir." The others need "de": "Il est nécessaire DE partir."
ne pas avoir le droit de
On n’a pas le droit de manger ici.
Il ne faut pas perdre ton badge.

"Il ne faut pas" = YOU MUSTN’T (it’s forbidden / not a good idea). "Il n’est pas nécessaire" / "tu n’as pas à" = YOU DON’T NEED TO. Romanian "nu trebuie" covers both meanings; French separates them (like English "mustn’t" / "don’t have to").
In principle you leave at six.
You don’t need to come if you’re tired.
"The train was supposed to arrive at noon." (according to the timetable)
Le train était censé arriver à midi.
Le train était obligé d’arriver à midi.
Le train avait à arriver à midi.
Qui est la tutrice de Radu ?

Are we allowed to eat here?

On 1 January, at noon, Nathalie had arranged to meet Ioana outside the door of Atelier Rhône. It was cold, the street was empty, and the whole city was still asleep after New Year’s Eve. Nathalie was holding a small parcel wrapped in brown paper and a screwdriver.

"It has to be you who puts it up," she said, handing her the parcel. "It’s tradition." Inside was a brand-new brass plaque, which read: "Atelier Rhône — N. Fabre & I. Moreau-Popescu, architects". Ioana had to try three times to get the first screw in.

When the plaque was fixed, they stood looking at it for a moment, side by side, in silence. Then Nathalie took out of her bag two plastic cups and a small bottle of champagne. "I know, it’s midday and it’s a public holiday," she said. "But it’s better to start the year with a good habit."

Ioana sent a photo of the plaque to the whole family. The fastest reply came from Iași: the grandmother had had the photo printed at the village photographer’s and had already hung it in the kitchen, next to the icon. Elena had written: "Your grandmother is showing your name to all the neighbours. You have to come this summer, otherwise she’ll start organising tours."

A week later, on Monday 8 January, Radu turned up at the same door at a quarter past eight. He was forty-five minutes early. He was wearing his tie, a shirt ironed by Lucia, and a rucksack full of pencils he had sharpened the night before, one by one, like a schoolboy on the first day of term.

He waited on the pavement, looking at the plaque. His sister’s name, in gold letters. He took a photo too, and sent it to his parents with a single word: "Pride". Then he realised he was standing outside the office where his sister would be his boss, and he became a little less proud, and a lot more nervous.

Chloé arrived at five to nine, by bike, her cheeks red. She was a tall blonde girl of twenty-three, very calm, who spoke little and drew like an angel. She came from Grenoble and didn’t know anyone in Lyon. Radu held out his hand with a smile: "Welcome. I didn’t know anyone either, two years ago."

The morning was devoted to the rules. Nathalie explained everything, from the badge to the coffee machine. Then she showed them round: the big room with the drawing tables, the model room, the little kitchen with the rules pinned on the wall, and Ioana’s office at the back, with a window that looked out over the rooftops.

In the afternoon, Ioana called Radu into her office. She had spread out on the table the drawing he had shown Nathalie in November, the one of the La Duchère room. She looked at it for a long time, a red pencil in her hand. Then she began to speak, in a voice Radu had never heard her use. A professional’s voice.

"It’s a lovely idea," she said. "But it isn’t a project. The windows are too big: in summer, the children will roast. There’s no emergency exit. The toilets are at the other end of the building. And you’ve forgotten that you need wheelchair access. It’s compulsory."

With each remark, she drew a red line across the drawing. After twenty minutes, there was almost nothing left of the original. Radu said nothing. He gritted his teeth. He felt like answering back, defending himself, reminding her that she used to pinch his pencils when they were little. But he remembered the rule: accept criticism without arguing.

"You’ll have to start again," Ioana concluded. "You have to hand in three sketches on Friday. One with smaller windows, one with the stage in the middle, one with two separate rooms. And it’s essential that you follow the standards. I’m giving you the safety regulations. Read them tonight."

She handed him a binder as thick as a dictionary. Radu took it without a word and left the office. In the big room, Chloé watched him go past with his binder and his drawing covered in red. She said nothing. But at lunchtime she came and sat next to him in the kitchen.

"My tutor did the same to me this morning," she said, opening her salad box. "Nathalie crossed out half my portfolio. I think it’s their method. They knock us down on the first day to see if we get back up." Radu smiled for the first time since the start of the afternoon.

That evening he got home very late. Lucia was waiting for him with a plate of pasta. He showed her the red drawing. She looked at it with an architect’s eyes. "She’s right about everything," she said gently. "The windows, the toilets, the access. Everything." Radu sighed. "I know. That’s the worst part."

For four days he worked as never before. He arrived at half past eight and left last, which meant he had to turn off the lights and close the windows, as article 5 required. In the evenings he read the safety regulations in bed, until Lucia took the binder out of his hands and switched off the lamp.

Ioana came by twice a day. She looked at his sketches, asked a question, sometimes drew a small line, rarely in red. She never paid him a compliment. Only once, on Thursday evening, looking at the third sketch, did she say: "That’s not bad." Then she left. Radu felt as if he had won a prize.

On Friday at five o’clock, he put his three sketches on his sister’s desk. She laid them out side by side and studied them in silence for what felt like an eternity. Then she looked up at him. For the first time that week, she was smiling. Not like a tutor. Like a big sister.

"The third one," she said. "The one with two rooms. That’s the one we’ll present to Claire on Monday. You’ve done in four days what some architects don’t do in a month." She stood up and hugged him. "And now I’m your sister again until nine o’clock on Monday. We’re going to eat at our place."

Radu wanted to say something clever, something professional. But all he managed to say was: "You destroyed me on Monday." Ioana laughed. "I know. I had to. If I’d told you it was brilliant, you’d have handed in a dangerous project. And Nathalie would have killed me."

On Saturday, the whole family went up to Fourvière to see Hélène. She had been better since her cold ended, but she was still tired and rarely left her room. She received them in her armchair by the window, with a shawl around her shoulders and a big smile.

Rose-Hélène was ten months old now. She couldn’t walk yet, but she could stand by holding on to the furniture, and she went round the room holding on to the bed, the table, the armchair. When she reached Hélène, she grabbed her knees and looked at her triumphantly.

"Soon," said Hélène, stroking her hair. "Soon you’ll let go and walk all by yourself. And I have to be there that day. Do you hear me, darling? You have to wait for me." Rose-Hélène replied with a long, incomprehensible speech that made everyone laugh.

Radu told them about his first week, exaggerating a little. The red lines, the safety binder, the coffee rule. Hélène laughed until she cried. When he mentioned the three sketches, she asked to see them. Radu had them in his rucksack, of course. He never let them out of his sight.

Hélène looked at the third sketch for a very long time, her glasses on the end of her nose. The two rooms, the little stage, the lower windows, a corner marked "buckets". Then she put a finger on a spot on the drawing. "And what’s this here?" Radu went red. "It’s a bench. Under a tree. In front of the entrance."

"So that the parents can wait for their children," he explained. "And so that the grandparents can listen to the rehearsals through the window when the weather’s nice." Hélène said nothing. She took off her glasses and wiped her eyes with the embroidered handkerchief she always kept up her sleeve.

"You have to promise me one thing," she said at last. "When the room is built, you’ll plant a lime tree. Not another tree. A lime tree." Radu promised. He didn’t ask why. Ioana and Julien looked at each other. They both knew which tree the bench in the 1962 photo stood under.

On the way home, in the funicular, Radu took out his pencil and added a word to the sketch, next to the bench: "lime tree". Then he underlined it twice. Rose-Hélène, asleep in Julien’s arms, was still holding the little button from Hélène’s jacket, which she had pulled off without anyone noticing.

On Monday morning, at a quarter to nine, Radu was outside the door again. He looked at the gold plaque, his sister’s name. Then he imagined, just below it, another plaque, much smaller, which didn’t exist yet. He smiled, swiped his badge, and went in.

The office’s internal rules are pinned on the kitchen wall. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
Article 1. Working hours are from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. If you are late, it is essential to phone your tutor before 9 a.m.
Article 2. It is strictly forbidden to eat or drink in front of the computers and next to the models. Coffee is drunk in the kitchen. No exceptions.
Article 3. Every employee must wear their badge. Without a badge, you can’t get in, get out or use the printer. It’s better not to lose it.
Article 4. Team meetings take place every Monday at 9.30. Everyone is supposed to attend, interns included. Everyone has to present the progress of their project.
Article 5. The last person to leave must turn off the lights and close the windows. There is no need to water the plants: Nathalie takes care of them.
Article 6. It is compulsory to celebrate everyone’s birthday with a cake. The cake must be home-made or bought at Sophie’s. Industrial cakes are forbidden.
